# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Drapesk Deal Team
**From:** [Associate]
**Re:** Project Cobalt Lantern: Issues in the Kestrin Cell Reclamation deal papers
**Documents reviewed:**
- Stock Purchase Agreement dated March 9, 2026 (the "SPA")
- Drapesk Board Unanimous Written Consent dated March 6, 2026 (the "Board Consent")
- Seller Disclosure Schedule (the "Schedule")
- Closing logistics email thread, April 14–21, 2026

---

## Executive Summary

Drapesk is buying 100% of Kestrin Cell Reclamation, Inc. from Trepal Holdings Corp. for **$184,000,000** (SPA §2.1). **$9,200,000** goes into indemnity escrow (§2.3). New York law governs (§11.8).

The Board Consent says the Company's principal liability exposure is environmental (Recital 1.2). The SPA as drafted largely fails to protect Drapesk against that exposure, for four reasons:

1. **Environmental representation is capped.** The environmental representation (§4.14) is not a Fundamental Representation. Breaches of it therefore fall under the **10% of the Purchase Price ($18.4 million) cap**. This contradicts the terms the Board approved.
2. **Environmental claims may be time-barred before they can be brought.** The 6-month survival period can expire before Drapesk is even permitted to bring an environmental claim.
3. **Drapesk gives Seller an uncapped indemnity for pre-Closing operations.** This is effectively a reverse indemnity that can claw back Drapesk's own environmental recoveries.
4. **Seller may assign freely and be released.** Seller can assign the Agreement to anyone, including its indemnity and its non-compete and feedstock covenants, and is then released.

Several secondary points compound these problems: the escrow release timing, the remediation standard, the consultant's independence, and Board authority. These follow below.

**Timing caveat.** The SPA was signed on March 9, 2026. The email thread schedules Closing for April 23, 2026. Any fix now requires a written amendment signed by both parties (§11.4), and Seller has no obligation to agree. If Closing has already occurred on April 23, 2026, the key dates have likely passed or are imminent:
- Phase II Report deadline: October 20, 2026
- General survival expiry: October 23, 2026
- Escrow release: on or about October 30, 2026

Please confirm the Closing status immediately (see Part C). If Closing has occurred, protective action on environmental claims is urgent.

---

## A. Principal Issues (in order of significance)

### Issue 1: Environmental representation omitted from "Fundamental Representations," so environmental losses are capped at 10%

**Where:**
- SPA §1.1 (definition of "Fundamental Representations")
- Schedule §1.1(f)
- SPA §9.4(a)
- Contrast with Board Consent, Resolution 2(c)

**What the documents say:**
- SPA §1.1 does not list the Fundamental Representations itself. It defines them as the Article IV representations "listed in Section 1.1(f) of the Disclosure Schedule."
- Schedule §1.1(f) says "the Fundamental Representations shall consist of Sections 4.1, 4.2, 4.3 and 4.5." That covers Organization, Authority, Capitalization and Brokers. **Section 4.14 (Environmental Matters) is omitted.**
- Under SPA §9.4(a), Seller's liability under §9.2(a) is capped at **10% of the Purchase Price ($18,400,000)**. The cap does not apply to Fundamental Representations or Fraud.
- Environmental breaches are therefore capped. They also get only the 6-month survival period under §9.1, rather than statute of limitations plus 60 days, and they are subject to the $920,000 Basket under §9.4(b).
- The Board approved the deal on the express term that the Fundamental Representations "include Section 4.14 (Environmental Matters)" (Resolution 2(c)).

**Why §11.9 does not fix this:** The order-of-precedence clause in §11.9 applies only where the SPA body and the Schedule *conflict*. They do not conflict here. The SPA body delegates the content of the definition to the Schedule, and §1.2 makes the Schedule part of the Agreement. A New York court would read the two together and apply the Schedule's list. Under the SPA as drafted, §4.14 is **not** a Fundamental Representation.

**Why it matters to Drapesk:**
- Environmental liability is the largest risk in a battery recycling business. Examples include soil or groundwater contamination from electrolyte leachate, releases from black-mass storage, and PFAS and metals in wastewater.
- The Phase II scope covers three Facilities and includes 13 or more groundwater monitoring wells (Schedule §6.8). Remediation costs at that scale can easily exceed $18.4 million.
- Above the cap, Drapesk's main fallback is the Company's Pollution Legal Liability policy ($25 million, Meridale, Schedule §4.17). Seller's recovery is reduced by any insurance proceeds received (§9.4(e)).
- The deal also departs from the Board-approved terms. See Issue 8 on officer authority.

**Recommendation:**
- Raise this with Seller's counsel (Jonah Reidel, Ashbury Kline & Sorensen) as a drafting error that conflicts with the agreed term sheet. Ask for a written amendment under §11.4 that names the Fundamental Representations in the SPA body, so they no longer depend on the Schedule. Proposed language:

  > "**Fundamental Representations**" means the representations and warranties of Seller set forth in Sections 4.1 (Organization), 4.2 (Authority), 4.3 (Capitalization), 4.5 (Brokers) and 4.14 (Environmental Matters).

- Delete Schedule §1.1(f), or conform it to the new definition.
- Ask for any drafts of the Schedule shown to the Board (Board Consent §1.3(a)). If the draft listed §4.14, that strengthens a request for reformation for mutual mistake. If Seller refuses, that is a fallback argument, not a substitute for the amendment.
- If Seller will not make §4.14 fundamental, the minimum fallback is:
  - a separate, higher environmental cap (for example, the full Purchase Price);
  - a standalone environmental indemnity for pre-Closing conditions that is not subject to the Basket; and
  - an extended survival period (see Issue 2).

  Any such fallback needs Board sign-off, because it departs from Resolution 2(c).

---

### Issue 2: Survival gap means the environmental claim window may never open

**Where:** SPA §9.1, read together with §9.6 and §6.8. The 6-month escrow release in §9.7 makes the problem worse.

**What the documents say:**
- Because §4.14 is not fundamental (Issue 1), it survives only "until the date that is six (6) months after the Closing Date" (§9.1). Claims must be noticed before that date.
- Buyer "shall not deliver a Claim Notice with respect to any inaccuracy in or breach of Section 4.14 until thirty (30) days after Buyer's receipt of the Phase II Report" (§9.6).
- Seller's consultant must deliver the Phase II Report "no later than 180 days after the Closing Date" (§6.8). That is roughly the same point as six months.
- If the report arrives late in the 180-day period, the survival period expires before the 30-day Environmental Review Period ends.
- Even if the report arrives early, Drapesk has only a short window, and Seller controls the report's timing through its own consultant.
- Illustration with an April 23, 2026 Closing:
  - Report deadline: October 20, 2026
  - Earliest permitted Claim Notice: about November 19, 2026
  - Survival expiry: October 23, 2026
- New York courts generally enforce contractual survival periods that shorten the time to sue. A court would likely enforce this gap as written.

**Why it matters to Drapesk:**
- Drapesk's most important representation could become unenforceable in practice.
- The §9.1 savings clause covers only claims noticed *before* expiry, and §9.6 bars giving that notice.
- The escrow is released to Seller "within five (5) Business Days after the date that is six (6) months after the Closing Date" (§9.7). No environmental claim can be pending at that point to hold back funds, so the $9.2 million escrow will typically be gone before any environmental claim is made.

**Recommendation:**
- In the same amendment as Issue 1:
  - Make §4.14 survive until 60 days after the applicable statute of limitations (as a Fundamental Representation). At minimum, it should survive no less than 36 months after Closing.
  - Delete the §9.6 bar on Claim Notices. Alternatively, add a tolling clause. Proposed language:

    > "Notwithstanding Section 9.1, the survival period applicable to Section 4.14 shall not expire earlier than ninety (90) days after the later of (i) Buyer's receipt of the Phase II Report and (ii) the expiration of the Environmental Review Period, and any Claim Notice delivered within such period shall be timely."

  - Allow Buyer to deliver a protective Claim Notice at any time, with the meet-and-confer process running in parallel.
  - Revise §9.7 so the escrow, or an environmental holdback, is not released until the extended environmental claim window closes.
- **If Closing has occurred and no amendment is in place:**
  - Deliver a protective Claim Notice under §9.5(a) at once, describing all known environmental facts. The §9.6 prohibition may be challenged, but a protective notice preserves the argument.
  - Ask Seller for a written tolling and standstill agreement.
  - Instruct the Escrow Agent not to release funds without joint instructions. Note that §9.7 obliges Drapesk to sign them.
  - Confirm whether the Phase II Report has been delivered and when.

---

### Issue 3: Uncapped Buyer indemnity for pre-Closing Company operations

**Where:** SPA §9.3(b) and §9.4(c)

**What the documents say:**
- Buyer must indemnify Seller Indemnitees for all Losses arising from "the ownership or operation of the Company or any of the Facilities, **whether before or after the Closing**" (§9.3(b)).
- Buyer's 10% cap applies to Buyer's indemnity "other than with respect to Section 9.3(b)" (§9.4(c)). §9.3(b) is therefore uncapped.
- The Basket and survival limits do not restrict §9.3(b). It is not a representation-based claim, so it survives under the covenant rule in §9.1.

**Why it matters to Drapesk:**
- Drapesk takes on unlimited liability for the Company's *historical* liabilities, including the pre-Closing contamination that Seller warrants against in §4.14.
- The clause is circular. If Drapesk recovers from Seller under §9.2(a) for a pre-Closing environmental breach, Seller can claim the same Losses back from Drapesk under §9.3(b), without limit.
- It also exposes Drapesk to uncapped claims by third parties or regulators against Trepal as the former owner or operator. One example is CERCLA "owner/operator at time of disposal" liability.
- This undercuts the whole value of Seller's indemnity.

**Recommendation:** Amend §9.3(b) so it covers only the post-Closing period and excludes anything Seller indemnifies:

> "(b) the ownership or operation of the Company or any of the Facilities **after the Closing**, except to the extent such Losses arise out of any matter for which Seller is obligated to indemnify any Buyer Indemnitee under Section 9.2 (determined without regard to the Cap, the Basket or any survival period) or any condition existing at or prior to the Closing;"

Also delete "other than with respect to Section 9.3(b)" from §9.4(c), so the Buyer cap applies. This is a market-standard point, and Seller should have little basis to resist it.

---

### Issue 4: Seller can assign freely and be released, including its indemnity and restrictive covenants

**Where:** SPA §11.5

**What the documents say:**
- Buyer cannot assign without Seller's consent.
- "Seller may assign this Agreement or any of its rights or obligations hereunder to any Person without the consent of Buyer." Once the assignee delivers a written assumption, "Seller shall thereupon be released from such obligations."
- There is no creditworthiness test, no bar on assignment to a competitor, and no continuing guarantee.

**Why it matters to Drapesk:**
- Seller's **Article IX indemnity** could be moved to an unfunded shell, for example once the escrow is released under §9.7. Drapesk would then have no creditworthy party to claim against.
- The **5-year non-compete and spent-battery feedstock covenant** in §6.10 could be assigned to a competing battery recycler, or to a party that cannot deliver feedstock. That defeats part of the goodwill Drapesk is paying for.
- The release from Seller eliminates Drapesk's recourse against Trepal entirely.

**Recommendation:** Amend §11.5 so the assignment rules are mutual:

> "Neither party may assign this Agreement or any of its rights or obligations hereunder without the prior written consent of the other party, and any purported assignment in violation of this Section 11.5 shall be void. No assignment shall relieve the assigning party of any of its obligations hereunder."

If Seller insists on flexibility, the fallback is:
- assignment only to a creditworthy Affiliate, with Seller remaining jointly and severally liable; and
- an express prohibition on assigning §6.10 obligations, or assigning to any Person engaged in a competing business.

Consider also requesting a parent guarantee or a creditworthiness covenant from Trepal.

---

## B. Secondary Issues

### Issue 5: Remediation to the "least stringent standard"

**Where:** SPA §9.6, last sentence

**Why it matters:** Remediation of any environmental claim must use the least stringent standard allowed for continued industrial use. This limits Drapesk's recovery and may require deed restrictions or engineering controls. It can also leave residual contamination that lowers property value, hampers financing, or breaches the Reno lease (a leased Facility, Schedule §4.10).

**Recommendation:** Replace it with a standard that is "required by Environmental Law or any Governmental Authority, and reasonably acceptable to Buyer." Also require that Buyer controls remediation at Facilities it owns or operates.

### Issue 6: Phase II controlled by Seller's consultant; no pre-signing invasive sampling

**Where:**
- SPA §1.1 ("Environmental Consultant")
- SPA §6.8 and §6.2
- Schedule §6.8 and §4.14(f)
- Board Consent Resolution 2(d)

**Why it matters:**
- The Board approved an *independent* consultant. The SPA instead names Halvorsen Ridge, which Seller engages and which prepared all three of Seller's Phase I reports.
- Drapesk could not sample before Closing without Seller's consent (§6.2).
- Seller controls the scope, timing and (indirectly) the findings of the Phase II, and that report is the gateway to Drapesk's environmental claims under §9.6.

**Recommendation:**
- Obtain Drapesk's right to approve the consultant, or to engage its own consultant jointly.
- Ask for Buyer participation in, and copies of, all field data as it is produced.
- Ask for a firm, earlier delivery date, with Buyer's claims tolled if the report is late.
- Reserve Buyer's right to do its own sampling after Closing without waiting for the Phase II.

### Issue 7: Escrow size and release

**Where:** SPA §2.3 and §9.7

**Why it matters:**
- The $9,200,000 escrow is only 5% of the Purchase Price and half of the $18.4 million cap.
- It is released at six months, before environmental claims can be made (Issue 2).
- After release, Drapesk must look to Trepal directly (§9.8), and Trepal could assign away its obligations (Issue 4).

**Recommendation:**
- Add a separate environmental holdback, released only after the Phase II findings are resolved, or extend the escrow term.
- Consider adding a parent guarantee.

### Issue 8: Board authority and closing certificates

**Where:**
- Board Consent Resolution 3 and Resolution 2(c)
- SPA §5.2, §3.3(c) and §7.3

**Why it matters:**
- Authorized Officers may approve changes only "consistent with the principal terms" in Section 2 of the Board Consent.
- The executed SPA departs from Resolution 2(c) on the environmental representation, its cap and its survival. It also contains terms the Board was not told about, such as the uncapped §9.3(b) indemnity.
- This raises a question whether execution was within the officers' authority.
- At Closing, Drapesk's Secretary must certify the Board resolutions (§3.3(c)), and Drapesk represents due authorization (§5.2).
- Seller is unlikely to challenge authority, but the inconsistency is a governance and fiduciary concern for the Drapesk Board.

**Recommendation:**
- Before Closing, either obtain the amendment described in Issues 1–4, or brief the Board and obtain a supplemental consent that approves or ratifies the terms as they actually stand.
- Do not deliver the Secretary's certificate until this is resolved.

### Issue 9: No standalone pre-Closing environmental indemnity

**Where:** SPA §9.2

**Why it matters:**
- Seller's environmental exposure rests entirely on the §4.14 representation, which is subject to the cap, the Basket and the survival period.
- Some sub-clauses also depend on the Disclosure Schedule. The 4.14(d) items in the Schedule, such as the stormwater basin and process tanks, are carved out of the representation.
- Contamination that Drapesk knew about, or that the Phase II identifies, should be covered by a specific indemnity rather than litigated as a breach of representation.

**Recommendation:** Add a §9.2(d) indemnity covering Losses from any Hazardous Materials condition existing at or before Closing at any current or former Facility, and from any off-site disposal arranged before Closing. It should not be subject to the Basket and should have a long survival period.

---

## C. Closing Logistics (email thread)

The thread is largely in order:
- The funds flow ($184,000,000 less $9,200,000 escrow = $174,800,000 to Seller) matches §§2.1–2.3.
- The wire instructions were verified by phone at the letterhead number.
- Third-party consents (Sagebrush, Northgate) are reported received.
- The post-Closing notices list matches Schedule §§4.4 and 4.11.

Points to note:
- **The thread does not address any of Issues 1–9.** Elena's message proposes releasing signature pages and wires on April 23, 2026. Those steps should be **held until the amendment is signed**, or until the Board has knowingly accepted the current terms. If Drapesk closes without the amendment, it loses most of its leverage.
- Drapesk proposes Ingrid Tolvanen and Rafael Szymczak as site contacts for the Phase II. Both are "Knowledge of Seller" individuals (Schedule §1.1(k)). Drapesk should appoint its own representative to attend the Phase II field work as well.
- The Reno Facility is leased. Confirm that the landlord consent signed April 10 does not contain environmental covenants or restoration obligations that interact with Issue 5.

---

## D. Matters That Cannot Be Resolved From These Files

1. **Closing status.** I need to know whether Closing occurred on April 23, 2026, and whether any amendment was signed. If Closing has occurred, I also need:
   - the date the Phase II Report was delivered;
   - any Claim Notices already given; and
   - the escrow balance and release status.
2. **The draft Disclosure Schedule given to the Board** (Board Consent §1.3(a)) and the counsel term summary (§1.3(b)). These show whether §4.14 appeared in the draft §1.1(f), which is relevant to a mutual mistake argument and to negotiating leverage.
3. **Negotiation history.** Any markups or emails showing how §§9.3(b), 9.6 and 11.5 entered the draft.
4. **Environmental diligence.** The Phase I reports and the September 2025 EHS audit (Schedule §4.14(f)), and the advisors' presentation to the Board. These are needed to size the likely exposure against the $18.4 million cap and the $25 million Pollution Legal Liability policy.
5. **The Pollution Legal Liability policy terms** (Meridale PLL-30-019874). I need its change-of-control provisions, whether Drapesk will be an insured after Closing, and its exclusions for known conditions. Under §9.4(e), insurance proceeds reduce Seller's liability.
6. **Trepal's financial condition** and any affiliate structure, to assess the risk of an assignment to a weaker entity (Issue 4) and the need for a guarantee.
7. **The executed Escrow Agreement** (Exhibit A form), to confirm the release mechanics and whether a holdback is possible.

Please let me know how you would like to proceed with Seller's counsel. I can circulate a draft amendment covering Issues 1–6 on request.

# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Deal Team, Drapesk Materials Group, Inc. acquisition of Kestrin Cell Reclamation, Inc.
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 5, 2026
**Re:** Pre-closing review of deal papers. Stock Purchase Agreement with Trepal Holdings Corp. dated March 9, 2026

---

## Executive Summary

Drapesk is buying all 1,000 outstanding Shares of Kestrin from Trepal for a Purchase Price of **$184,000,000** (SPA §2.1). Of that amount, **$9,200,000** goes to Calloway Trust Bank, N.A. as the Indemnity Escrow Amount (SPA §2.3). The SPA is governed by New York law (SPA §11.8).

I reviewed four documents:

- the SPA;
- Drapesk's board written consent dated March 6, 2026;
- Seller's Disclosure Schedule; and
- the closing logistics email thread from April 14 to 21, 2026.

The papers allocate environmental risk in a way that differs materially from what Drapesk's board approved. They also leave Drapesk exposed to two structural problems:

- an uncapped reverse indemnity in Seller's favor; and
- an unrestricted right for Seller to assign its obligations.

**Timing caveat.** The email thread shows closing set for April 23, 2026. Nothing in the folder confirms whether closing occurred.

- **If it has not occurred,** each fix below can be raised as a pre-signing or pre-closing point.
- **If it has occurred,** each fix requires a written amendment signed by both parties (SPA §11.4), and Seller has little incentive to agree.

Please confirm the deal's status. The items below are ranked by significance.

---

## Issue 1. Environmental representation left out of "Fundamental Representations," so environmental claims fall under the 10% Cap

**Where:**
- SPA §1.1, definition of "Fundamental Representations"
- Disclosure Schedule §1.1(f)
- SPA §9.4(a)
- Board Consent, Resolution 2(c)

**What the documents say:**
- SPA §1.1 does not list the Fundamental Representations. It defines them as the Article IV sections "listed in Section 1.1(f) of the Disclosure Schedule."
- Disclosure Schedule §1.1(f) states that "the Fundamental Representations shall consist of Sections 4.1, 4.2, 4.3 and 4.5." These are Organization, Authority, Capitalization and Brokers. Section 4.14 (Environmental Matters) is not on the list.
- SPA §9.4(a) caps Seller's liability under §9.2(a) at **10% of the Purchase Price ($18,400,000)**. The Cap does not apply to Fundamental Representations or Fraud.

**Why it matters to Drapesk:**
- As drafted, a breach of §4.14 is a capped, general representation claim. It is also subject to the $920,000 Basket in §9.4(b).
- Drapesk's board found that "the Company's principal liability exposure relates to environmental matters" (Board Consent ¶1.2). Examples include contaminated black-mass storage areas and electrolyte leachate reaching groundwater.
- The board approved the deal expressly "on the basis of" the principal terms in Resolution 2. Resolution 2(c) lists §4.14 as a Fundamental Representation, excluded from the cap.
- Soil and groundwater remediation at three battery-recycling sites could easily exceed $18.4 million. The Pollution Legal Liability policy (Disclosure Schedule §4.17) has a $25,000,000 aggregate limit. Under SPA §9.4(e), Losses are calculated net of insurance proceeds, but the policy does not replace a full indemnity.

**The precedence clause does not fix this.** SPA §11.9 makes the SPA body prevail only where there is a "conflict or inconsistency" between the body and the Disclosure Schedule. There is none here. The body hands the definition to the schedule, and the schedule fills it in. A New York court would read the two together and apply the schedule's list as written. Drapesk should not assume §4.14 is fundamental under the current text.

**Board authority concern:**
- Resolution 3 authorizes officers to sign the Purchase Agreement and approve changes only where these are "consistent with the principal terms in Section 2."
- An SPA that leaves §4.14 out of the Fundamental Representations is not consistent with Resolution 2(c).
- The Buyer Secretary's certificate (SPA §3.3(c)) and Drapesk's authority representation (SPA §5.2) both rest on that consent.

**Recommendation:**
1. Amend SPA §1.1 to list the Fundamental Representations directly in the body of the agreement, with no cross-reference to the schedule:
   > "'Fundamental Representations' means the representations and warranties of Seller set forth in Sections 4.1 (Organization), 4.2 (Authority), 4.3 (Capitalization), 4.5 (Brokers) and 4.14 (Environmental Matters)."
2. Delete or conform Disclosure Schedule §1.1(f).
3. Raise this with Ashbury Kline as a conforming correction that reflects the agreed deal. If Seller refuses, escalate to Drapesk management.
4. If Seller will not agree, the variance must go back to the Drapesk board for a supplemental consent before signing or closing. Signing on these terms falls outside the officers' delegated authority.
5. **Further information needed:**
   - Term sheet or negotiation history showing whether Seller agreed to treat §4.14 as fundamental.
   - Confirmation of which draft schedule the board saw (Board Consent ¶1.3(a)).

---

## Issue 2. Buyer gives Seller an uncapped indemnity for pre-Closing Company operations

**Where:** SPA §9.3(b) and §9.4(c)

**What the documents say:**
- Under SPA §9.3(b), Buyer indemnifies the Seller Indemnitees for all Losses arising from "the ownership or operation of the Company or any of the Facilities, **whether before or after the Closing**."
- SPA §9.4(c) caps Buyer's aggregate liability at 10% of the Purchase Price "other than with respect to Section 9.3(b)."

**Why it matters to Drapesk:**
- Read together, these sections make Drapesk liable, **without limit**, for Kestrin's historical liabilities incurred while Trepal owned it. Pre-Closing environmental contamination is the main example.
- That is the same risk Seller warrants against in §4.14 and indemnifies under §9.2(a).
- The two indemnities point in opposite directions. Any amount Drapesk recovers from Seller for a pre-Closing environmental breach could be claimed back by Seller under §9.3(b), and Seller's claim would be uncapped.
- Third parties (regulators, neighbors, CERCLA claimants) may pursue Trepal as former owner or operator. Drapesk would then owe Trepal full indemnity for those claims.
- The clause largely cancels Seller's environmental indemnity and adds open-ended exposure on top of the Purchase Price.

**Recommendation:**
1. Revise §9.3(b) as follows:
   > "(b) the ownership or operation of the Company or any of the Facilities **after the Closing**, except to the extent such Losses arise out of any matter for which Seller is obligated to indemnify any Buyer Indemnitee under Section 9.2 (without giving effect to the Cap, the Basket or any survival limitation)."
2. Delete "other than with respect to Section 9.3(b)" from §9.4(c), so that Buyer's 10% cap applies to all of §9.3.
3. Add an express statement that Buyer's indemnity does not extend to any Losses that arise from facts or conditions existing at or before Closing.

---

## Issue 3. Seller may assign freely and be released from its obligations

**Where:** SPA §11.5

**What the documents say:**
- Buyer may not assign without Seller's consent.
- Seller, by contrast, "may assign this Agreement or any of its rights or obligations hereunder to any Person without the consent of Buyer."
- Once the assignee delivers a written assumption, Seller "shall thereupon be released" from those obligations.

**Why it matters to Drapesk:** Seller's obligations after Closing are the main source of Drapesk's protection. They include:

- the Article IX indemnity, including the Fundamental Representation and tax indemnity in §9.2(c);
- the post-Closing Phase II obligation in §6.8;
- confidentiality under §6.6; and
- the 5-year non-compete and spent-battery feedstock covenant in §6.10.

Under §11.5, Trepal could take any of the following steps:

- move its indemnity obligations to a thinly capitalized affiliate or shell, and walk away. This matters most once the Escrow Fund is released to Seller under §9.7, because direct recovery from Seller under §9.8 would then be worthless;
- assign the §6.10(b) feedstock covenant, and Seller's rights under it, to a competing battery recycler. This would undermine the goodwill Drapesk is paying for; and
- assign the §6.8 Phase II obligation to an entity with no means of funding it.

Nothing in the clause requires the assignee to be creditworthy, to be an affiliate, or to be a non-competitor. The clause is also one-sided, which makes it a reasonable point to push back on.

**Recommendation:** Replace the third sentence of §11.5 with mutual language:

> "Neither party may assign this Agreement or any of its rights or obligations hereunder without the prior written consent of the other party, except that either party may assign its rights (but not its obligations) to an Affiliate, provided that no such assignment shall relieve the assigning party of any of its obligations hereunder. Any purported assignment in violation of this Section 11.5 shall be null and void."

If Seller insists on keeping some flexibility, Drapesk's fallback position should include all of the following:

- (a) Seller remains jointly and severally liable after any assignment;
- (b) no assignment of any kind to a Person engaged in the businesses described in §6.10(a);
- (c) any assignee must meet a minimum net-worth test or provide a parent guaranty; and
- (d) the §6.10 covenants cannot be assigned separately from the rest of the Agreement.

---

## Issue 4. The Escrow is small and short relative to the risk

**Where:** SPA §2.3, §9.7 and §9.8

**Why it matters to Drapesk:**
- The $9,200,000 escrow equals 5% of the Purchase Price. That is half the $18,400,000 Cap.
- The escrow is released to Seller about six months after Closing, less any amounts claimed in pending Claim Notices (§9.7).
- After release, Drapesk's recovery depends on Seller's credit (§9.8). Combined with Issue 3, that credit could be moved to an assignee.

**Recommendation:**
1. Seek an increase in the escrow, or a separate environmental escrow or holdback sized to the environmental advisors' remediation estimates.
2. Seek a later release date.
3. Alternatively, require a Trepal parent guaranty or other credit support.
4. **Further information needed:**
   - Trepal's financial statements and creditworthiness.
   - Drapesk's environmental advisors' cost estimates presented to the board (Board Consent ¶1.3(c)).

---

## Issue 5. Phase II consultant independence and the remediation standard

**Where:**
- SPA §1.1, definition of "Environmental Consultant"
- SPA §6.8 and §9.6
- Disclosure Schedule §6.8 and §4.14(f)
- Email thread, Messages 7 and 8

**Why it matters to Drapesk:**
- Board Resolution 2(d) contemplates an "independent environmental consultant." The SPA instead names Halvorsen Ridge Environmental, LLC, which Seller engages. Halvorsen also prepared Seller's own Phase I reports (Disclosure Schedule §4.14(f), items 1–3).
- The email thread names Ingrid Tolvanen and Rafael Szymczak as Halvorsen's site contacts. Both are "Knowledge of Seller" individuals under Disclosure Schedule §1.1(k), and Mr. Szymczak is the Company's EHS Director. The people who would know about pre-existing contamination would therefore be guiding the field work.
- SPA §9.6 limits any remediation to "the least stringent standard permitted ... for the continued industrial use of the relevant Facility." This restricts Drapesk's Losses even where a regulator, a lender or a landlord (for example, Sagebrush at the Reno lease) requires a stricter cleanup.

**Recommendation:**
1. Give Buyer joint control of the consultant's engagement and scope, or a right to approve them.
2. Give Buyer the right to have its own consultant observe and split-sample.
3. Require the consultant to owe reliance and duties to Buyer.
4. Name Drapesk-appointed site contacts rather than Seller-knowledge individuals.
5. Revise the §9.6 remediation standard to "the standard required by applicable Environmental Law, any Governmental Authority or any lease or Environmental Permit governing the relevant Facility."

## Issue 6. Seller can veto invasive sampling before Closing

**Where:** SPA §6.2

**Why it matters to Drapesk:** Seller's prior written consent is required for any invasive sampling before Closing. As a result, Drapesk may close without any intrusive environmental data of its own, relying instead on Seller's Phase I reports and the post-Closing Phase II.

**Recommendation:**
1. If closing has not occurred, ask Seller to consent to targeted pre-Closing sampling at the black-mass storage and electrolyte drainage areas. Henderson and Chandler are the priority sites.
2. At a minimum, confirm with Drapesk's environmental advisors that the Phase I reports identified no recognized environmental conditions that warrant sampling before Closing.

## Issue 7. Status of the Pollution Legal Liability policy after the change of control

**Where:** SPA §4.17; Disclosure Schedule §4.17 (Meridale policy PLL-30-019874, term April 1, 2024 – April 1, 2029)

**Why it matters to Drapesk:**
- The $25,000,000 PLL policy is Drapesk's most important backstop for environmental losses.
- Many PLL policies end coverage or require insurer consent when the insured changes control.
- Because Losses are calculated net of insurance (SPA §9.4(e)), the status of this policy also affects how Seller's indemnity works in practice.

**Recommendation:**
1. Obtain and review the policy for change-of-control, named-insured and retroactive-date provisions.
2. If needed, obtain the insurer's consent or an endorsement before Closing.
3. **Further information needed:** a copy of the policy. It is not in the folder.
